BFS.summary: BFS explores a graph level by level using a queue, visiting nodes in order of distance from the start.
BFS.problem: It finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and systematically explores neighbors before going deeper.
BFS.mechanics: Enqueue the start node and mark visited. While the queue is not empty, dequeue u, process neighbors of u, and enqueue each unseen neighbor while recording parent/distance. Layers expand until the goal is found or the frontier empties.
BFS.tradeoffs: BFS uses more memory than DFS for wide frontiers; DFS may find a deep solution sooner but not the shortest unweighted path. Dijkstra/A* replace BFS when edges have weights.
BFS.troubleshoot: If BFS never finishes, check missing visited marks (infinite graphs/cycles) or exploding branching. If distances look wrong, verify you only enqueue on first visit and that the graph edges are correct.
BFS.integration: 1) Model the domain as an adjacency list. 2) Implement BFS with explicit visited. 3) Unit-test distance on a tiny graph. 4) Cap queue size / depth for production safety.

Big-O complexity.summary: Big-O describes an upper bound on how an algorithm's cost grows with input size n (asymptotic worst-case growth class).
Big-O complexity.problem: It lets you compare algorithms independently of machine speed and reject designs that blow up as data scales.
Big-O complexity.mechanics: Count dominant operations as n grows, drop constants and lower-order terms, and classify the growth. Nested loops over n often yield O(n²); halving search space each step yields O(log n).
Big-O complexity.tradeoffs: Big-O ignores constants that matter at small n and real caches/IO. Prefer Big-Theta when you mean tight bound; use profiling for hot paths where constants dominate.
Big-O complexity.troubleshoot: If production latency grows unexpectedly, measure with increasing n, check for hidden O(n²) (nested scans, N+1 queries), and confirm you are not measuring fixed overhead.
Big-O complexity.example:
# binary search O(log n) vs linear O(n)
def find(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == x: return mid
        if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1
    return -1
Big-O complexity.integration: 1) State complexity in design docs for hot paths. 2) Add a scale test with 10× data. 3) Fail CI if p95 exceeds budget after growth.

binary search.summary: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array by repeatedly discarding half of the remaining range.
binary search.problem: It turns O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups when data is ordered and random-access.
binary search.mechanics: While lo ≤ hi, compute mid, compare a[mid] to the target, and move lo or hi to shrink the half that cannot contain the answer. Generalize to binary search on a monotonic predicate (search the answer space).
binary search.tradeoffs: Requires sorted (or monotonic) data; sorting first may dominate. Prefer hash sets for exact membership when order is irrelevant and memory allows.
binary search.troubleshoot: Off-by-one bugs show as infinite loops or missed edges—trace lo/hi on a 2-element array. Confirm sort order and stable lower_bound semantics for duplicates.
binary search.example:
def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid
    return lo
binary search.integration: 1) Ensure data is kept sorted or indexed. 2) Use library binary search when available. 3) Add tests for empty, one element, duplicates, and missing values.

divide and conquer.summary: Divide and conquer splits a problem into independent subproblems, solves them, then combines results (e.g., mergesort, quicksort, binary search).
divide and conquer.problem: It unlocks O(n log n) sorting and parallelizable workloads by reducing problem size recursively.
divide and conquer.mechanics: Define a base case, partition input, recurse on parts, then merge. Mergesort divides then merges in linear time per level across log n levels.
divide and conquer.tradeoffs: Recursion depth and combine cost can dominate; sometimes iterative DP or greedy is simpler. Quicksort’s average is great but worst-case is O(n²) without care.
divide and conquer.troubleshoot: Stack overflows imply missing base cases or unbalanced splits. Wrong results usually come from incorrect combine logic—test on tiny inputs.
divide and conquer.integration: 1) Write the recurrence and expected complexity. 2) Implement with clear base cases. 3) Compare against a known-good sort on random arrays.

dynamic programming.summary: Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems with optimal substructure by memoizing or tabulating sub-results.
dynamic programming.problem: It avoids exponential recompute in problems like knapsack, edit distance, and path counting.
dynamic programming.mechanics: Define state (what a subproblem answers), base cases, and transitions. Either recurse with a cache (top-down) or fill a table in dependency order (bottom-up).
dynamic programming.tradeoffs: DP uses extra memory and needs a correct state; greedy is simpler when a local choice is provably safe. Sometimes Dijkstra/BFS replaces DP on graphs.
dynamic programming.troubleshoot: Wrong answers usually mean an incomplete state (missing a dimension) or iteration order bugs. Profile memory for large tables; compress state when possible.
dynamic programming.integration: 1) Write state/transition on paper. 2) Implement memoized recursion for clarity. 3) Convert hot paths to iterative tables. 4) Add property tests vs brute force on small n.

sorting algorithms.summary: Sorting algorithms reorder elements by a key; common ones are mergesort, quicksort, heapsort, and timsort (used by Python).
sorting algorithms.problem: Sorted data enables binary search, ordered reports, and efficient merges of streams.
sorting algorithms.mechanics: Comparison sorts repeatedly compare keys; mergesort is stable O(n log n); quicksort partitions around a pivot; Python’s timsort exploits runs. Counting/radix sorts beat O(n log n) for restricted keys.
sorting algorithms.tradeoffs: Stability matters when sorting by multiple keys. In-place quicksort saves memory but is not stable. For nearly sorted data, adaptive sorts win.
sorting algorithms.troubleshoot: If order looks wrong, check comparator consistency (must be a total order). For performance regressions, measure n and check you accidentally used O(n²) sort.
sorting algorithms.example: rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r['last'], r['first']))  # stable multi-key in Python
sorting algorithms.integration: 1) Prefer language built-ins. 2) Document stability needs. 3) Benchmark on production-shaped data before custom sorts.

HTTP methods.summary: HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS) define the intent of a request on a resource.
HTTP methods.problem: They standardize safe/idempotent semantics so caches, proxies, and clients behave correctly.
HTTP methods.mechanics: Client sends method + URL + headers/body. Servers route by method. GET/HEAD should not change state; PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST often creates or triggers non-idempotent work.
HTTP methods.tradeoffs: Misusing POST for everything breaks caching and retry safety. PUT vs PATCH depends on whether the client sends a full replacement or a partial update.
HTTP methods.troubleshoot: Debug with curl -v: check method, status, and whether intermediaries strip bodies. Retries causing duplicates usually mean non-idempotent POST without idempotency keys.
HTTP methods.example:
curl -i -X GET https://api.example.com/users/42
curl -i -X POST https://api.example.com/users -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Ada"}'
HTTP methods.integration: 1) Define resource URLs and method semantics in an OpenAPI spec. 2) Enforce in framework routing. 3) Add contract tests for idempotency on PUT/DELETE.

HTTP caching.summary: HTTP caching stores responses so repeat requests can be served from cache using headers like Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified.
HTTP caching.problem: It cuts latency and origin load for cacheable GET responses.
HTTP caching.mechanics: Origin sets freshness (max-age) and validators. Caches serve fresh responses; on revalidation a 304 avoids transferring the body. Vary selects the correct variant for different request headers.
HTTP caching.tradeoffs: Aggressive caching can serve stale personalized data—use private for user-specific responses. Fine-grained invalidation is hard; prefer short TTL + ETag for dynamic APIs.
HTTP caching.troubleshoot: If users see stale content, inspect Cache-Control/Age, CDN rules, and Vary. If origin is overloaded, check that GETs are actually cacheable and not accidentally no-store.
HTTP caching.example:
Cache-Control: public, max-age=60
ETag: "abc123"
# client revalidate:
# If-None-Match: "abc123" → 304 Not Modified
HTTP caching.integration: 1) Classify endpoints as public/private. 2) Set Cache-Control + ETag on GETs. 3) Purge CDN on deploy for HTML. 4) Monitor cache hit ratio.

TLS.summary: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts and authenticates network connections so HTTP becomes HTTPS.
TLS.problem: It protects confidentiality and integrity against eavesdropping and tampering on the path.
TLS.mechanics: Client and server negotiate a cipher suite, server presents a certificate chain, client verifies it to a trust store, then both derive session keys and encrypt application data.
TLS.tradeoffs: TLS adds CPU and latency (mitigated by session resumption/HTTP/2). Certificate mismanagement causes outages. mTLS adds client certificates for service identity.
TLS.troubleshoot: Handshake failures: check clock skew, chain completeness, SNI hostname, and TLS version. Use openssl s_client to inspect the presented chain.
TLS.example: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject
TLS.integration: 1) Terminate TLS at a trusted edge. 2) Automate cert renewal (ACM/Let’s Encrypt). 3) Redirect HTTP→HTTPS and enable HSTS. 4) Alert on expiry within 14 days.

TCP.summary: TCP is a reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport protocol that provides streams with retransmission and congestion control.
TCP.problem: It is the default for HTTP, databases, and most apps that need all bytes delivered in order.
TCP.mechanics: After the three-way handshake, peers exchange segments with sequence numbers; lost data is retransmitted; receive windows prevent overrun; congestion control paces sends.
TCP.tradeoffs: TCP latency suffers from head-of-line blocking; UDP/QUIC may fit real-time or loss-tolerant workloads. Connection setup cost matters for tiny RPCs.
TCP.troubleshoot: Timeouts and resets: check firewalls, SYN floods, and half-open states with ss/netstat. Throughput issues often involve window size, packet loss, or bufferbloat.
TCP.example:
ss -tan | head
# ESTAB shows established TCP sessions with local/remote addresses
TCP.integration: 1) Prefer TCP libraries/HTTP stacks over raw sockets. 2) Set sane timeouts and retries. 3) Monitor retransmits and connection error rates.

TCP three-way handshake.summary: The TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) synchronizes sequence numbers and establishes a connection before data transfer.
TCP three-way handshake.problem: It prevents half-open confusion and agrees initial sequence numbers for reliable delivery.
TCP three-way handshake.mechanics: Client sends SYN with its ISN; server replies SYN-ACK with its ISN and ack; client sends ACK. Both sides then mark the connection ESTABLISHED.
TCP three-way handshake.tradeoffs: Handshakes add one RTT before data (mitigated by TCP Fast Open / TLS 1.3 0-RTT carefully). UDP skips this but loses reliability.
TCP three-way handshake.troubleshoot: SYN floods fill backlog queues—tune somaxconn/syn cookies. Connection timeouts often mean packets dropped by security groups or wrong bind address.
TCP three-way handshake.example:
# capture handshake (needs privileges)
# sudo tcpdump -ni any 'tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0'
TCP three-way handshake.integration: 1) Ensure listeners bind correctly. 2) Open firewall for SYN to the service port. 3) Alert on elevated SYN_RECV counts.

DNS resolution.summary: DNS resolution maps human domain names to IP addresses (and other records) via a hierarchy of resolvers and authoritative servers.
DNS resolution.problem: Without DNS, clients cannot find services by name; misconfigured DNS causes widespread outages.
DNS resolution.mechanics: App asks OS stub → recursive resolver queries root/TLD/authoritative as needed → caches answers for TTL → returns A/AAAA (or follows CNAME).
DNS resolution.tradeoffs: Low TTL speeds failover but increases query load; high TTL caches stale records after cutovers. CNAMEs at apex have restrictions.
DNS resolution.troubleshoot: NXDOMAIN vs SERVFAIL vs timeouts point to different layers. Compare dig @8.8.8.8 vs corporate resolvers; check split-horizon DNS.
DNS resolution.example:
dig +short example.com A
dig example.com NS
dig +trace example.com
DNS resolution.integration: 1) Document critical records and TTLs. 2) Dual-provision before cutover. 3) Lower TTL ahead of migrations. 4) Monitor resolution failure rates.

commit.summary: A Git commit is an immutable snapshot of the project tree plus metadata (author, message, parent pointer(s)).
commit.problem: Commits form history so teams can review, bisect, revert, and collaborate safely.
commit.mechanics: Staging selects content; commit writes a new object referencing the tree and parent. Branches are movable pointers to commits.
commit.tradeoffs: Small focused commits ease review; huge commits hide intent. Rewriting published history (force push) endangers collaborators.
commit.troubleshoot: If a commit is missing files, check what was staged. Lost work often sits on another branch or reflog—use git reflog before panicking.
commit.example:
git add -p && git commit -m "fix: handle empty DNS responses"
git log --oneline -5
commit.integration: 1) Agree on commit message conventions. 2) Prefer small commits. 3) Protect main from force-push. 4) Require review before merge.

branching.summary: A Git branch is a movable pointer to a commit, letting you diverge history for features, fixes, or releases.
branching.problem: Branches isolate in-progress work so main stays releasable.
branching.mechanics: Creating a branch names the current commit; new commits advance that pointer. Merging or rebasing integrates histories back.
branching.tradeoffs: Long-lived branches drift and hurt merges; trunk-based development keeps branches short. Release branches trade isolation for merge cost.
branching.troubleshoot: Diverged branches need merge/rebase. If you cannot find work, list branches and use reflog. Delete stale remote branches intentionally.
branching.example:
git switch -c feature/dns-ttl
git push -u origin HEAD
branching.integration: 1) Use short-lived feature branches. 2) Name by ticket/intent. 3) Delete after merge. 4) Protect main with required checks.

merge.summary: Git merge joins two histories, creating a merge commit when needed (or fast-forwarding when possible).
merge.problem: It integrates completed work while preserving parallel history.
merge.mechanics: Git finds a common ancestor, diffs both sides, and combines changes. Conflicting hunks must be resolved manually, then committed.
merge.tradeoffs: Merge preserves true history; rebase linearizes but rewrites commits. Prefer merge commits for shared branches if your team wants explicit integration points.
merge.troubleshoot: Repeated conflicts mean overlapping long-lived branches—rebase/merge more often. Use git status and mergetool during conflicts.
merge.example:
git switch main && git pull
git merge feature/dns-ttl
# resolve conflicts, then: git commit
merge.integration: 1) Keep branches fresh with main. 2) Resolve conflicts with tests green. 3) Prefer squash or merge per team policy. 4) Never force-push shared merges casually.

REST.summary: REST is an architectural style for networked APIs using resources identified by URLs, manipulated via HTTP methods and representations.
REST.problem: It provides a uniform, cacheable, loosely coupled interface between clients and servers.
REST.mechanics: Design nouns as resources (/orders/42), use methods for actions, return appropriate status codes, and keep servers stateless—session lives in tokens/DB, not server memory per request.
REST.tradeoffs: Pure REST can be chatty; GraphQL/RPC may fit complex client-driven queries. Over-rigid REST theater wastes time—be pragmatic about hypermedia.
REST.troubleshoot: Ambiguous endpoints and verbs cause client bugs—document status codes and idempotency. Debug with HTTP traces and contract tests.
REST.integration: 1) Publish OpenAPI. 2) Standardize error shape. 3) Version carefully. 4) Add consumer-driven contract tests.

cookies.summary: HTTP cookies are small name/value pairs the server sets via Set-Cookie and the browser stores and resends on later requests to the same site scope.
cookies.problem: They implement sessions and preferences without stuffing every URL with state.
cookies.mechanics: Server sends Set-Cookie; browser stores subject to attributes; matching requests include Cookie header. HttpOnly blocks JS access; SameSite mitigates CSRF; Secure requires HTTPS.
cookies.tradeoffs: Cookies are sent automatically—easy sessions, easy CSRF if SameSite/lax policies are wrong. Tokens in localStorage avoid CSRF but worsen XSS impact.
cookies.troubleshoot: Missing cookies: check Domain/Path/Secure and third-party blocking. Bloated headers: reduce cookie count/size.
cookies.example: Set-Cookie: session=abc; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
cookies.integration: 1) Prefer HttpOnly Secure session cookies. 2) Set SameSite deliberately. 3) Rotate session IDs on login. 4) Document CSRF strategy.

XSS.summary: Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects attacker-controlled script into pages viewed by other users, stealing sessions or performing actions as the victim.
XSS.problem: It breaks the browser’s trust that HTML/JS from your origin is safe.
concepts: stored vs reflected vs DOM XSS
XSS.mechanics: Untrusted input is reflected into HTML/JS/URL contexts without encoding. Fix by context-aware encoding, avoiding innerHTML with raw input, and CSP to limit script sources.
XSS.tradeoffs: Rich-text HTML requires careful sanitization allowlists. CSP helps but is not a substitute for encoding.
XSS.troubleshoot: Reproduce with a benign payload, find the sink (innerHTML, dangerous templating), and verify CSP reports. Check whether session cookies are HttpOnly.
XSS.example:
// Bad: el.innerHTML = userComment
// Good: el.textContent = userComment
XSS.integration: 1) Default-encode all untrusted output. 2) Add CSP with nonce/hash. 3) HttpOnly sessions. 4) Add security tests for reflective sinks.

SQL injection.summary: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into SQL, letting attackers alter query structure.
SQL injection.problem: It can leak, modify, or delete data and sometimes escalate to OS commands via DB features.
SQL injection.mechanics: Attacker supplies input that closes quotes and adds OR 1=1/-- etc. Prevent by binding parameters always; never string-build SQL with user data.
SQL injection.tradeoffs: Dynamic identifiers (table names) cannot be parameterized—use allowlists. ORMs help but raw SQL must still bind values.
SQL injection.troubleshoot: Hunt via code search for string-built SQL; test with benign payloads in staging. Review DB logs for unexpected statements.
SQL injection.example:
# Bad: f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id={user_id}"
# Good:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=%s", (user_id,))
SQL injection.integration: 1) Ban string-interpolated SQL in lint/review. 2) Use parameterized APIs only. 3) DB user with minimal grants. 4) Add SAST and penetration checks.

authentication.summary: Authentication verifies who a principal is (user/service), typically via passwords, tokens, certificates, or SSO.
authentication.problem: It is the gate before authorization; without it, identity-based access control is meaningless.
authentication.mechanics: User presents credentials; server verifies (e.g., argon2id hash compare) and establishes a session cookie or issues JWTs. MFA adds a second factor. Federated login delegates identity to an IdP.
authentication.tradeoffs: JWTs are scalable but harder to revoke; server sessions reverse that trade-off. Never store recoverable passwords.
authentication.troubleshoot: Login failures: distinguish user-enumeration carefully, check clock skew for JWTs, cookie flags, and redirect URIs for OAuth.
authentication.integration: 1) Use a vetted auth library. 2) Hash passwords with argon2/bcrypt. 3) Enforce MFA for privileged users. 4) Log auth events without secrets.

array.summary: An array (or list) stores elements in a contiguous, indexable sequence supporting random access by position.
array.problem: It is the default collection for ordered data and the basis of many algorithms.
array.mechanics: Elements live in order; indexing jumps by size×index. Dynamic arrays resize geometrically when capacity is exceeded, amortizing copy cost.
array.tradeoffs: Linked lists win rare middle insert patterns but lose cache performance. For frequent keyed lookup, prefer hash maps.
array.troubleshoot: Off-by-one and mutation-during-iteration are common bugs—copy or iterate indices carefully.
array.integration: 1) Prefer arrays/lists as default. 2) Pre-size when length known. 3) Document mutability expectations in APIs.

hash table.summary: A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function and buckets for average O(1) lookup, insert, and delete.
hash table.problem: It powers dictionaries, sets, caches, and indexes when you need keyed access.
hash table.mechanics: Hash(key) selects a bucket; collisions use chaining or open addressing. On high load factor, the table resizes and rehashes.
hash table.tradeoffs: Worst-case can degrade without good hashing; keys must be immutable for stability. Ordered maps or trees if you need sorted keys.
hash table.troubleshoot: Unexpected misses: check equality/hash consistency. Hot keys and poor hashes cause uneven buckets—profile.
hash table.integration: 1) Use language dict/map. 2) Ensure keys are hashable. 3) Watch memory for large maps. 4) Consider LRU caches for bounded memory.

hashing.summary: Hashing maps arbitrary data to a fixed-size digest for tables, integrity checks, or password storage (with slow KDFs).
hashing.problem: It enables fast equality checks and detects tampering when used cryptographically.
hashing.mechanics: A hash function mixes input bits into a digest. For hash tables, speed matters; for security, use SHA-256/BLAKE3; for passwords, use argon2 with unique salts—not raw SHA.
hashing.tradeoffs: Hashes are one-way (ideally); encryption is reversible with a key. Checksums like CRC are not cryptographic.
hashing.troubleshoot: Collision or verification failures: confirm canonical encoding (UTF-8, newlines) and algorithm match on both sides.
hashing.integration: 1) Pick algorithm by purpose (table vs integrity vs passwords). 2) Version digests in protocols. 3) Never roll your own crypto.

stack.summary: A stack is a LIFO collection: push and pop only at the top—used for call stacks, parsers, and undo.
stack.problem: It models nested structure and depth-first control flow naturally.
stack.mechanics: Push adds to top; pop removes top. Recursion uses the machine call stack; you can simulate DFS with an explicit stack.
stack.tradeoffs: Queues (FIFO) fit scheduling/BFS. Stacks do not give fair ordering of oldest items.
stack.troubleshoot: Overflows imply unbounded nesting—cap depth. Wrong pop order usually means mismatched push/pop in parsing.
stack.integration: 1) Use stacks for nested parsing/undo. 2) Bound depth. 3) Prefer clear iterative stacks when recursion depth is risky.

heap.summary: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array that keeps the min (or max) at the root for O(log n) insert/remove and O(1) peek.
heap.problem: It implements priority queues for schedulers, Dijkstra, and top-k problems.
heap.mechanics: Insert at end and sift up; remove root by swapping with last and sifting down. Array indexing uses parent/child formulas.
heap.tradeoffs: Heaps do not keep full sorted order—only the extreme. For arbitrary delete/decrease-key, more advanced heaps or trees may help.
heap.troubleshoot: Wrong order: verify comparator direction (min vs max). Ties may need secondary keys for stability.
heap.example:
import heapq
h = []
heapq.heappush(h, (2, 'b'))
heapq.heappush(h, (1, 'a'))
heapq.heappop(h)  # (1, 'a')
heap.integration: 1) Use stdlib heap/priority queue. 2) Store (priority, tiebreaker, value). 3) Test empty-pop behavior.

binary search tree.summary: A BST stores keys so left subtree < node < right, enabling average O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced.
binary search tree.problem: It maintains sorted order for range queries unlike hash tables.
binary search tree.mechanics: Search compares and branches left/right. Insert walks to a leaf position. Unbalanced inserts degrade to O(n); balanced trees rotate to keep height logarithmic.
binary search tree.tradeoffs: Hash maps are faster for exact lookup without order. B-trees dominate disk-backed DB indexes.
binary search tree.troubleshoot: Failed finds after insert: check duplicates policy and comparator. Degenerate trees: switch to balanced trees or shuffle inserts.
binary search tree.integration: 1) Prefer language TreeMap / sorted containers when order matters. 2) Document comparator. 3) Avoid rolling your own production BST.

trie.summary: A trie (prefix tree) stores strings by sharing character prefixes for fast prefix search and autocomplete.
trie.problem: It answers “words with prefix P” efficiently compared to scanning a list.
trie.mechanics: Insert walks/creates nodes per character and marks terminal. Lookup follows characters; prefix search explores a subtree.
trie.tradeoffs: Tries use more memory than hash sets for sparse alphabets; radix trees compress chains. For huge dictionaries, specialized structures or FM-indexes appear.
trie.troubleshoot: Wrong misses: normalization (case/Unicode) mismatches. Memory blowups: compress or limit alphabet.
trie.integration: 1) Normalize input Unicode. 2) Use a trie for autocomplete/prefix features. 3) Cap dictionary size and measure memory.

graph representation.summary: Graphs are stored as adjacency lists (usual) or matrices; lists map each vertex to neighbor edges.
graph representation.problem: Representation choice drives memory and algorithm speed for BFS/DFS/shortest paths.
graph representation.mechanics: Build list: for each edge u→v, append v to adj[u] (and u to adj[v] if undirected). Matrices use O(n²) space and O(1) edge checks.
graph representation.tradeoffs: Matrices suit dense graphs/Floyd-Warshall; lists suit sparse graphs. Choose immutable snapshots if concurrent mutation is hard.
graph representation.troubleshoot: Missing edges or double edges: validate input. Index vs labeled nodes: keep a stable id map.
graph representation.integration: 1) Pick list vs matrix from density. 2) Encapsulate behind helpers. 3) Property-test round-trips from edge lists.

recursion.summary: Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs until a base case.
recursion.problem: It expresses trees, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking clearly.
recursion.mechanics: Each call pushes a frame; base case returns; frames unwind combining results. Any recursion can be rewritten with an explicit stack.
recursion.tradeoffs: Deep recursion risks overflows—prefer iteration for deep linear chains. Memoize when subproblems overlap.
recursion.troubleshoot: Infinite recursion: missing/incorrect base case. Wrong results: check whether state is mutated across calls.
recursion.integration: 1) Write base cases first. 2) Test depth limits. 3) Convert hot deep recursion to iterative form.

process.summary: A process is an OS instance of a running program with its own address space, handles, and scheduling entity (plus threads).
process.problem: Processes isolate faults and security boundaries between programs.
process.mechanics: OS creates a process (fork/exec or CreateProcess), loads the image, and schedules it. Threads share the address space; processes generally do not.
process.tradeoffs: Threads are lighter for shared-memory concurrency; processes give stronger isolation (browsers, workers).
process.troubleshoot: Zombies mean parents did not wait; leaks of FDs show as EMFILE. Use ps/lsof to inspect.
process.integration: 1) Prefer processes for isolation boundaries. 2) Handle SIGCHLD/wait. 3) Cap FD usage. 4) Supervise with systemd/k8s.

mutex.summary: A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) ensures only one thread holds a critical section at a time.
mutex.problem: It prevents race conditions on shared mutable state.
mutex.mechanics: Thread acquires mutex before touching shared data and releases after. If held, others block until unlock. Always unlock via finally/RAII.
mutex.tradeoffs: Coarse locks hurt scalability; lock-free structures are harder. Prefer message passing when possible.
mutex.troubleshoot: Deadlocks: lock ordering and timeouts. Contended locks: profile wait time and shrink critical sections.
mutex.example:
import threading
lock = threading.Lock()
with lock:
    shared += 1
mutex.integration: 1) Identify shared mutable state. 2) Protect with clear lock scopes. 3) Document lock order. 4) Add race tests (TSan) where available.

deadlock.summary: Deadlock is a permanent wait cycle where each party holds a resource another needs (Coffman: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait).
deadlock.problem: It freezes progress until process kill or timeout intervention.
deadlock.mechanics: Prevent by acquiring locks in global order, using try-lock timeouts, or avoiding nested locks. Detect via wait-for graphs in DB engines.
deadlock.tradeoffs: Fine-grained locking raises deadlock risk vs coarse locks. Sometimes queues eliminate shared locks.
deadlock.troubleshoot: Symptoms: threads stuck, DB error 40P01. Capture lock graphs; reproduce with concurrency stress.
deadlock.example:
-- Postgres
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock';
deadlock.integration: 1) Define lock order. 2) Keep transactions short. 3) Use deadlock retries for DBs. 4) Alert on rising wait events.

race condition.summary: A race condition means outcome depends on unsafe timing/interleaving of concurrent operations on shared state.
race condition.problem: It causes Heisenbugs: lost updates, duplicate charges, torn reads.
race condition.mechanics: Two threads read-modify-write without sync; both write stale values. Fix with mutexes, atomics, DB transactions/constraints, or single-threaded ownership.
race condition.tradeoffs: Over-synchronization hurts performance; under-synchronization corrupts data. Prefer immutability and actor models.
race condition.troubleshoot: Reproduce with stress tests and race detectors. Look for check-then-act on files/rows without locks or UNIQUE constraints.
race condition.example:
# Bad: if key not in cache: cache[key] = load()
# Better: use a lock or concurrent map compute-if-absent
race condition.integration: 1) Eliminate shared mutability where possible. 2) Add constraints at the DB. 3) Run concurrent tests. 4) Use race detectors in CI for C/C++/Go/Java.

context switching.summary: Context switching is the OS saving one thread/process CPU state and restoring another so many tasks share cores.
context switching.problem: It enables multitasking but costs cycles and cache warmth.
context switching.mechanics: Scheduler picks next task, saves old registers/PC, loads new ones, and resumes. Excessive switching thrashs caches.
context switching.tradeoffs: More threads than needed increase switch overhead. Blocking I/O models vs async change switch patterns.
context switching.troubleshoot: High system CPU with low useful work may mean thrashing—profile sched latency (perf, run queue).
context switching.integration: 1) Size worker pools to cores×factor. 2) Avoid busy-wait. 3) Measure p99 latency under load.

CPU scheduling.summary: CPU scheduling chooses which ready thread runs next on a core (CFS, priorities, real-time policies).
CPU scheduling.problem: It balances fairness, latency, and throughput for workloads sharing CPUs.
CPU scheduling.mechanics: On timer interrupt or blocking, scheduler picks next task by policy. Interactive tasks get lower latency; batch can yield throughput.
CPU scheduling.tradeoffs: Priority inversion and starvation need inheritance or careful classes. Pinning helps latency-sensitive apps but reduces packing.
CPU scheduling.troubleshoot: Starvation or latency spikes: check nice values, cgroup CPU limits, and noisy neighbors.
CPU scheduling.example:
ps -eo pid,ni,cmd --sort=ni | head
# cgroup CPU in containers often shows as throttling
CPU scheduling.integration: 1) Set appropriate nice/cgroup limits. 2) Isolate latency-critical services. 3) Monitor throttling metrics.

virtual memory.summary: Virtual memory gives each process a private virtual address space mapped to physical frames via page tables, with disk swap as backing.
virtual memory.problem: It isolates processes and lets programs use more memory than physical RAM (at a cost).
virtual memory.mechanics: CPU translates virtual→physical through page tables (cached in TLB). On miss/fault, OS loads a page or signals an error (segfault).
virtual memory.tradeoffs: Overcommit + swap can cause latency spikes; containers often disable swap. Huge pages reduce TLB pressure for big heaps.
virtual memory.troubleshoot: OOM kills and thrashing: watch si/so in vmstat and working set size. Segfaults: invalid pointers/mappings.
virtual memory.integration: 1) Size memory limits to working set. 2) Alert on swap activity. 3) Use huge pages only with measurement.

paging.summary: Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages mapped to frames, simplifying allocation vs variable segments.
paging.problem: It underpins virtual memory and protects processes from each other’s addresses.
paging.mechanics: OS allocates frames and fills page table entries. Demand paging loads pages on first access; COW shares pages until write.
paging.tradeoffs: Large page tables cost memory; huge pages trade flexibility. Fragmentation is less than with pure segments.
paging.troubleshoot: Major faults imply disk I/O—reduce working set or add RAM. Soft faults are cheaper remaps.
paging.example:
# major/minor faults on Linux
ps -o min_flt,maj_flt,cmd -p $$
paging.integration: 1) Measure fault rates under load. 2) Pre-touch critical heaps if needed. 3) Align mmap sizes thoughtfully.

filesystem.summary: A filesystem organizes bytes on storage into files, directories, permissions, and metadata (inodes).
filesystem.problem: Programs persist data through files rather than raw disk blocks.
filesystem.mechanics: Path lookup walks directories to an inode; read/write goes through page cache unless O_DIRECT. Mounts attach trees to devices or remote shares.
filesystem.tradeoffs: Different FS (ext4, XFS, ZFS) trade features/performance. Network FS add consistency quirks.
filesystem.troubleshoot: ENOSPC, permission denied, and stale NFS handles are common—check df -i for inode exhaustion too.
filesystem.integration: 1) Monitor disk and inode usage. 2) Separate volumes for data/logs. 3) Back up critical mounts. 4) Document mount options.

CPU registers.summary: CPU registers are tiny, fastest storage inside the core holding operands, addresses, and status during instruction execution.
CPU registers.problem: They make the instruction cycle possible; compilers allocate variables to registers when possible.
CPU registers.mechanics: Instructions read/write registers; spills go to stack memory when registers are exhausted. Interrupts save register state.
CPU registers.tradeoffs: More registers can improve speed but increase context-switch cost. You rarely manage them directly outside assembly.
CPU registers.troubleshoot: Debuggers show register state on crashes—use to diagnose calling-convention bugs in native code.
CPU registers.example:
# x86-64 example: rax holds return values in SysV ABI
# (inspect via gdb: info registers)
CPU registers.integration: 1) Prefer high-level languages. 2) For native hot paths, inspect compiler asm. 3) Follow ABI when writing assembly.

CPU instruction cycle.summary: The instruction cycle is fetch → decode → execute (plus memory access/writeback in pipelined CPUs).
CPU instruction cycle.problem: It is how programs progress: each instruction advances architectural state.
CPU instruction cycle.mechanics: PC points to next instruction; CPU fetches bytes, decodes opcode, executes, then updates PC. Pipelines overlap stages for throughput.
CPU instruction cycle.tradeoffs: Branch mispredicts and cache misses stall pipelines—algorithmic locality matters more than micro-optimizing asm early.
CPU instruction cycle.troubleshoot: Perf counters reveal stalls; focus on cache misses and branches before rewriting algorithms.
CPU instruction cycle.integration: 1) Write clear code first. 2) Profile before micro-optimizing. 3) Improve data locality for hot loops.

CPU cache hierarchy.summary: CPUs use L1/L2/L3 caches to keep recently used lines closer than DRAM, exploiting locality.
CPU cache hierarchy.problem: Cache-friendly layouts can yield order-of-magnitude speedups for tight loops.
CPU cache hierarchy.mechanics: On memory access, hardware checks L1→L2→L3→RAM. Lines are typically 64B. False sharing occurs when unrelated data share a line across cores.
CPU cache hierarchy.tradeoffs: Bigger caches help but cost power/area. Structure-of-arrays can beat array-of-structures for scans.
CPU cache hierarchy.troubleshoot: Perf cache-miss rates high: reorder loops, pack hot fields, align shared atomics to separate lines.
CPU cache hierarchy.example:
# pad to avoid false sharing (conceptually)
# struct { atomic_int counters[64]; }  # better: per-core counters
CPU cache hierarchy.integration: 1) Profile cache misses. 2) Keep hot data contiguous. 3) Avoid false sharing in concurrent counters.

RAM and persistent storage.summary: RAM is volatile, fast working memory; persistent storage (SSD/HDD) keeps data across power loss but is slower.
RAM and persistent storage.problem: Software must treat RAM as temporary and explicitly persist durable state.
RAM and persistent storage.mechanics: Reads/writes hit RAM; OS page cache may delay disk. Durability requires fsync/journal commits. Databases manage this carefully (WAL).
RAM and persistent storage.tradeoffs: Memory-first designs are fast but crash-lose data without persistence strategies. Disk-bound systems need batching.
RAM and persistent storage.troubleshoot: Data loss after crash: missing fsync or write barriers. Slow disks: check iostat and queue depths.
RAM and persistent storage.example:
iostat -xz 1 3
# ensure DB fsync settings match durability goals
RAM and persistent storage.integration: 1) Classify data as ephemeral vs durable. 2) Use DB/fsync correctly. 3) Monitor disk latency. 4) Test crash recovery.

binary representation.summary: Binary representation encodes values with bits (0/1); groups of 8 bits form a byte.
binary representation.problem: All digital data—numbers, text, images—ultimately is bits interpreted by a schema.
binary representation.mechanics: Positional powers of two form integers; formats define floating point and character encodings. Endianness decides byte order in memory/on wire.
binary representation.tradeoffs: Humans prefer hex for compactness. Wrong endianness or signedness causes subtle protocol bugs.
binary representation.troubleshoot: Mismatch dumps: print hex and confirm width/endian. Mask carefully to avoid sign extension bugs.
binary representation.integration: 1) Document binary layouts. 2) Use explicit endian helpers. 3) Add golden hex fixture tests.

two's complement.summary: Two’s complement encodes signed integers so addition/subtraction use the same hardware as unsigned, with the high bit as sign.
two's complement.problem: It is the universal signed integer representation in modern CPUs.
two's complement.mechanics: To negate, invert bits and add one. Overflow wraps modulo 2^n in unchecked arithmetic—define checked ops when needed.
two's complement.tradeoffs: Sign-magnitude is rarer; floating point is separate. Language “undefined behavior” on signed overflow in C/C++ differs from wrap in Java.
two's complement.troubleshoot: Unexpected negatives: unsigned/signed mix or byte decoding errors. Check casts.
two's complement.integration: 1) Prefer fixed-width types in protocols. 2) Test min/max edges. 3) Avoid mixing signed/unsigned carelessly.

character encoding and Unicode.summary: Character encoding maps characters to bytes; Unicode assigns code points, usually serialized as UTF-8.
character encoding and Unicode.problem: It prevents mojibake and enables multilingual text.
character encoding and Unicode.mechanics: UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per code point, ASCII-compatible. Decode bytes→str with known encoding; encode when writing. Normalize before comparing user-facing strings.
character encoding and Unicode.tradeoffs: Latin-1 mislabeled as UTF-8 causes errors. Some languages use UTF-16 internally (JS/Java) with surrogate pairs.
character encoding and Unicode.troubleshoot: Mojibake: wrong codec. Compare failures: normalize. Validate inputs reject invalid UTF-8.
character encoding and Unicode.integration: 1) Standardize on UTF-8 everywhere. 2) Declare charset in HTTP/HTML. 3) Normalize for search keys. 4) Reject invalid byte sequences.

OSI model.summary: The OSI model is a seven-layer conceptual stack (Physical→Application) for talking about networking responsibilities.
OSI model.problem: It helps locate bugs (L3 routing vs L4 ports vs L7 HTTP) even though real stacks are closer to TCP/IP.
OSI model.mechanics: Each layer adds headers (encapsulation) going down and strips them going up. Troubleshooting maps symptoms to layers.
OSI model.tradeoffs: OSI is pedagogical; do not force every product into seven boxes. TCP/IP four-layer model is often enough.
OSI model.troubleshoot: Map failures: link lights (L1), ARP (L2), ping (L3), connect (L4), HTTP status (L7).
OSI model.example:
# L3 vs L4 quick checks
ping -c1 8.8.8.8
nc -vz example.com 443
OSI model.integration: 1) Teach on-call the layer map. 2) Capture at the right layer. 3) Document trust boundaries per layer.

IPv4 subnetting.summary: IPv4 subnetting splits address space with a mask/CIDR prefix so hosts share a network and routers forward between networks.
IPv4 subnetting.problem: It structures addressing, controls broadcast domains, and enables routing policy.
IPv4 subnetting.mechanics: A /24 keeps 8 host bits (256 addresses, fewer usable). Hosts use mask to decide local vs route-via-gateway. Plan ranges to avoid overlaps in VPCs/VPNs.
IPv4 subnetting.tradeoffs: Smaller subnets waste fewer addresses but add routes; flat large subnets increase blast radius.
IPv4 subnetting.troubleshoot: Overlap causes asymmetric routing—audit CIDRs. Wrong mask yields “destination unreachable” for local peers.
IPv4 subnetting.example:
# 10.0.1.0/24 → mask 255.255.255.0
ipcalc 10.0.1.0/24 2>/dev/null || python3 - <<'PY'
import ipaddress
n=ipaddress.ip_network('10.0.1.0/24')
print(n.netmask, n.num_addresses)
PY
IPv4 subnetting.integration: 1) Plan non-overlapping CIDRs. 2) Document gateway/DNS. 3) Codify in Terraform. 4) Test connectivity matrices.

MAC address.summary: A MAC address is a 48-bit link-layer identifier for a network interface used within a L2 broadcast domain.
MAC address.problem: Switches forward frames by MAC; ARP maps IPv4→MAC on Ethernet.
MAC address.mechanics: Host ARP-requests for gateway MAC, then sends Ethernet frames with dest MAC. Routers strip L2 and forward IP to next hop L2.
MAC address.tradeoffs: MACs are not global routing identifiers. Virtualization and privacy features randomize MACs.
MAC address.troubleshoot: Duplicates confuse switches; check arp -an and CAM tables. Wireshark helps spot storms.
MAC address.example:
ip link show
ip neigh show
MAC address.integration: 1) Avoid duplicate MACs in labs. 2) Secure ARP where needed. 3) Rely on IP/DNS for app config, not MAC.

NAT.summary: Network Address Translation rewrites packet IP/ports so many private hosts share public IPs (or hide topology).
NAT.problem: It conserves IPv4 addresses and is standard at home/cloud edges.
NAT.mechanics: Outbound SNAT replaces private source with public IP and tracks ports; inbound DNAT forwards public ports to private hosts. State lives in conntrack.
NAT.tradeoffs: NAT breaks true end-to-end addressing (hurts some P2P). Prefer IPv6 or private connectivity for service meshes when possible.
NAT.troubleshoot: Outbound fails: check default route, masquerade rules, and conntrack table full. Inbound fails: security groups + DNAT mismatch.
NAT.example:
# Linux MASQUERADE sketch
# iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE
NAT.integration: 1) Centralize NAT at edge. 2) Monitor conntrack. 3) Prefer private links for east-west. 4) Document public port forwards.

socket.summary: A socket is an OS endpoint for network communication (IP:port + protocol) that apps read/write like a bidirectional channel.
socket.problem: It is the API between programs and TCP/UDP.
socket.mechanics: Servers bind+listen+accept; clients connect. Bytes stream on TCP sockets; datagrams on UDP. Close/shutdown manage half-close.
socket.tradeoffs: Higher-level HTTP clients hide sockets—use them unless you need custom protocols.
socket.troubleshoot: EADDRINUSE: port taken. Timeouts: set deadlines. TIME_WAIT piles: understand reuse options carefully.
socket.example:
python3 - <<'PY'
import socket
s=socket.create_connection(('example.com',80),5)
s.sendall(b'HEAD / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n')
print(s.recv(200)); s.close()
PY
socket.integration: 1) Prefer battle-tested client libraries. 2) Set timeouts. 3) Limit listen backlog. 4) Health-check accept loops.

load balancer.summary: A load balancer distributes traffic across multiple backends to improve availability and scale.
load balancer.problem: It avoids single-server bottlenecks and enables rolling updates.
load balancer.mechanics: LB receives connections, picks a healthy backend by policy, and proxies. Health checks remove bad targets. L7 can route by path/host.
load balancer.tradeoffs: Sticky sessions reduce stateless benefits. Over-complex L7 rules create outage risk—keep simple.
load balancer.troubleshoot: 502/504: backend dead or timeouts. Uneven load: check algorithm and slow instances. Verify health check paths.
load balancer.example:
# nginx upstream sketch
# upstream api { server 10.0.0.1; server 10.0.0.2; }
load balancer.integration: 1) Put LB in front of N≥2 healthy instances. 2) Tune health checks. 3) Drain on deploy. 4) Alert on unhealthy host count.

horizontal scaling.summary: Horizontal scaling adds more instances to handle load, versus vertical scaling which grows one machine.
horizontal scaling.problem: It improves capacity and fault isolation when the app is designed to be stateless or sharded.
horizontal scaling.mechanics: Run N replicas behind a load balancer; externalize sessions/cache/DB. Autoscale on CPU/RPS/queue depth with cooldown.
horizontal scaling.tradeoffs: Not all systems scale linearly—DB write bottlenecks dominate. Vertical may be cheaper until a cliff.
horizontal scaling.troubleshoot: Scaling out without effect: find serial bottlenecks (global locks, single shard). Watch cold-start and cache stampede.
horizontal scaling.integration: 1) Make services stateless. 2) Put shared state in managed stores. 3) Autoscale on meaningful SLIs. 4) Load test the data tier.

cache.summary: A cache stores recently or frequently used data closer/faster than the source of truth to cut latency and load.
cache.problem: It accelerates reads when freshness requirements allow.
cache.mechanics: On read, check cache; on miss, load origin and populate. Invalidate or expire entries when data changes. Cap size with eviction policy.
cache.tradeoffs: Stale reads vs complexity of invalidation. Write-through vs write-behind change durability/latency.
cache.troubleshoot: Stampede: many misses thundering origin—use singleflight/locks. Memory growth: set maxmemory/eviction.
cache.example: value = redis.get(key) or db.load(key) and redis.setex(key, 60, value)
cache.integration: 1) Identify hot read paths. 2) Choose TTL/invalidation. 3) Cap memory. 4) Measure hit rate and origin load.

message queue.summary: A message queue asynchronously decouples producers and consumers with durable or buffered messages (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ).
message queue.problem: It smooths load spikes and isolates failures between services.
message queue.mechanics: Producer enqueues; consumer pulls/processes/acks. Failures retry until DLQ. Design consumers idempotent because duplicates happen.
message queue.tradeoffs: Queues add operational complexity and eventual processing delay. Sync RPC is simpler for low-latency request/response.
message queue.troubleshoot: Lag growth: scale consumers or fix poison messages. Dupes: enforce idempotency keys.
message queue.example:
# SQS-style mental model
# receive → process → delete/ack; on crash, visibility timeout returns message
message queue.integration: 1) Pick queue tech for volume/ordering. 2) Make handlers idempotent. 3) Add DLQ + alerts on lag. 4) Load test retry storms.

virtual machine.summary: A virtual machine emulates a computer so guest OS kernels run isolated on a hypervisor atop physical hosts.
virtual machine.problem: It consolidates hardware and isolates tenants more strongly than processes alone.
virtual machine.mechanics: Hypervisor schedules vCPUs and mediates devices; guests think they own hardware. Images boot VMs; cloud APIs create them in minutes.
virtual machine.tradeoffs: VMs are heavier than containers; containers share a kernel. Use VMs for strong isolation/multi-OS; containers for app deploy density.
virtual machine.troubleshoot: Slow boots/noisy neighbors: check oversubscription and storage IOPS. Clock drift affects TLS/Kerberos.
virtual machine.example: # cloud mental model: choose AMI/image → instance type → subnet/SG → ssh/ssm
virtual machine.integration: 1) Standardize golden images. 2) Automate provisioning. 3) Patch via pipelines. 4) Monitor hypervisor-level metrics.

compiler.summary: A compiler translates source code into a lower-level form (bytecode or machine code) with analysis and optimizations.
compiler.problem: It catches many errors early and produces efficient executables/artifacts.
compiler.mechanics: Front end parses and checks; middle end optimizes IR; back end emits code. Interpreters execute more directly; JITs compile hot paths at runtime.
compiler.tradeoffs: Long compile times vs runtime performance. Dynamic languages trade safety for flexibility.
compiler.troubleshoot: Cryptic errors: reduce to minimal repro. ABI breaks: version modules carefully.
compiler.integration: 1) Enable warnings as errors in CI. 2) Pin toolchain versions. 3) Cache builds. 4) Test across supported targets.

garbage collection.summary: Garbage collection automatically reclaims heap objects no longer reachable, reducing manual free errors.
garbage collection.problem: It prevents many use-after-free bugs at the cost of pauses and CPU.
garbage collection.mechanics: Collector finds live objects from roots and reclaims the rest. Generational GCs exploit infant mortality. Tuning heap size affects frequency/pause.
garbage collection.tradeoffs: Manual memory can be tighter for embedded/hard realtime. RC (refcount) is predictable but cycles need handling.
garbage collection.troubleshoot: Latency spikes: profile GC pauses and allocation churn. Leaks still happen via unintended retained references.
garbage collection.example:
# Java example mindset: -Xmx, GC logs
# Node: clinic/heap snapshots for retained paths
garbage collection.integration: 1) Measure allocation hotspots. 2) Bound caches. 3) Tune heap with load tests. 4) Watch p99 during GC.

stack memory.summary: Stack memory holds function frames (locals, return addresses) and grows/shrinks automatically with calls.
stack memory.problem: It is fast and scoped to call lifetime, unlike heap allocations.
stack memory.mechanics: Call pushes frame; return pops. Large stack arrays risk overflow—use heap for big/variable lifetimes.
stack memory.tradeoffs: Thread stacks are finite; deep recursion is dangerous. Heap is shared and needs management/GC.
stack memory.troubleshoot: Stack overflow crashes: reduce depth or heap-allocate. Corruption: look for buffer overflows on stack buffers in native code.
stack memory.example:
# prefer heap for large buffers
buf = bytearray(10_000_000)
stack memory.integration: 1) Keep stack frames small. 2) Bound recursion. 3) Enable stack protectors in native builds.

scope and lifetime.summary: Scope is where a name is visible; lifetime is how long a value exists in memory.
scope and lifetime.problem: Confusing them causes use-after-free, leaks, and surprising closures.
scope and lifetime.mechanics: Locals exist for the call; heap objects until unreachable; closures extend lifetimes by retaining references.
scope and lifetime.tradeoffs: Long lifetimes increase memory; too-short lifetimes cause dangling references in native languages.
scope and lifetime.troubleshoot: Leaks: retained closures/caches. Dangling: pointers outliving owners—use ownership types/GC.
scope and lifetime.example:
def make():
    x = []
    def add(v): x.append(v); return x
    return add  # x lives with closure
scope and lifetime.integration: 1) Prefer tight scopes. 2) Avoid unintended captures. 3) Clear references when done with large graphs.

static typing.summary: Static typing checks types at compile/check time before runtime, catching whole classes of bugs early.
static typing.problem: It documents interfaces and enables better tooling/refactors.
static typing.mechanics: Annotate or infer types; compiler/typechecker rejects mismatches. Gradual systems (TypeScript/mypy) allow incremental adoption.
static typing.tradeoffs: Dynamic typing speeds prototyping but shifts errors to runtime. Overly complex types can slow teams.
static typing.troubleshoot: Type errors after refactor: fix at boundaries first. Escape hatches (any) hide bugs—minimize them.
static typing.example:
def area(w: float, h: float) -> float:
    return w * h
static typing.integration: 1) Enable typechecker in CI. 2) Type public APIs first. 3) Ban unchecked any in new code. 4) Generate types from OpenAPI when useful.

value semantics.summary: Value semantics means variables behave like independent values (copies); mutating one does not affect another.
value semantics.problem: It reduces aliasing bugs compared to shared references.
value semantics.mechanics: Languages copy small values; larger structures may be references. Immutable persistent structures give value-like safety with sharing.
value semantics.tradeoffs: Reference semantics are cheaper for big objects but create alias surprises. Be explicit at API boundaries.
value semantics.troubleshoot: Unexpected shared mutation: you passed a reference. Freeze/copy at boundaries.
value semantics.example: a = [1,2]; b = list(a); b.append(3)  # a unchanged
value semantics.integration: 1) Prefer immutable DTOs across threads. 2) Copy at trust boundaries. 3) Document mutability in APIs.

encapsulation.summary: Encapsulation hides internal representation behind a stable interface so callers depend on behavior, not fields.
encapsulation.problem: It limits blast radius of changes and preserves invariants.
encapsulation.mechanics: Keep fields private; expose methods that maintain invariants. Modules export a minimal surface.
encapsulation.tradeoffs: Over-encapsulation can yield anemic getters; under-encapsulation couples everything to fields.
encapsulation.troubleshoot: Broken invariants: find leaked mutable references. Tighten interfaces and add tests for invariants.
encapsulation.integration: 1) Make fields private by default. 2) Test invariants. 3) Review public API surface in PRs.

inheritance.summary: Inheritance lets a class derive behavior/structure from a parent, forming an is-a hierarchy.
inheritance.problem: It reuses code but can couple hierarchies if overused.
inheritance.mechanics: Child receives parent members; overrides specialize. Prefer shallow hierarchies; call super carefully.
inheritance.tradeoffs: Composition/interfaces often beat deep inheritance (fragile base class). Use inheritance for true behavioral subtypes.
inheritance.troubleshoot: LSP violations: child breaks parent expectations—favor interfaces and composition.
inheritance.integration: 1) Prefer composition. 2) Keep hierarchies shallow. 3) Enforce LSP with subtype tests.

polymorphism.summary: Polymorphism lets one interface handle many concrete types (runtime dispatch or generics).
polymorphism.problem: It enables extensibility without rewriting callers for each variant.
polymorphism.mechanics: Callers depend on an interface; concrete types implement it. Generics parameterize algorithms over types statically.
polymorphism.tradeoffs: Too many runtime types hurt clarity; switch statements may be simpler for closed sets (prefer sum types when available).
polymorphism.troubleshoot: Wrong method called: check vtables/overrides. Prefer explicit interfaces over duck typing at boundaries.
polymorphism.integration: 1) Define interfaces at boundaries. 2) Keep closed sets explicit. 3) Use generics for containers/algorithms.

interfaces and abstract classes.summary: Interfaces (and abstract classes) define required behaviors without committing to a full implementation.
interfaces and abstract classes.problem: They enable polymorphism and test doubles while keeping modules decoupled.
interfaces and abstract classes.mechanics: Declare methods a type must support; implementations provide behavior. Depend on abstractions in high-level modules.
interfaces and abstract classes.tradeoffs: Abstract classes can share code but couple inheritance; interfaces are thinner. Avoid interface bloat.
interfaces and abstract classes.troubleshoot: Missing methods fail compile/typecheck—good. Runtime surprises mean you used dynamic typing without checks.
interfaces and abstract classes.integration: 1) Introduce interfaces at volatile boundaries. 2) Keep them minimal. 3) Provide fakes for tests.

SOLID principles.summary: SOLID is five OOP design heuristics: SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP—guiding maintainable module boundaries.
SOLID principles.problem: They reduce brittle coupling as systems grow.
SOLID principles.mechanics: Keep modules focused; extend via new types; don’t break subtypes; prefer small interfaces; depend on abstractions. Apply pragmatically, not dogmatically.
SOLID principles.tradeoffs: Over-abstracting creates ceremony; under-applying creates spaghetti. Balance with YAGNI.
SOLID principles.troubleshoot: Painful changes spanning many classes signal SRP/DIP issues—redraw boundaries.
SOLID principles.example: # DIP: high-level OrderService depends on PaymentGateway interface, not StripeClient directly
SOLID principles.integration: 1) Review PRs for boundary smells. 2) Extract interfaces when third parties appear. 3) Refactor when change cost rises.

unit testing.summary: Unit tests verify a small unit (function/class) in isolation with fast, deterministic assertions.
unit testing.problem: They catch regressions early and document expected behavior.
unit testing.mechanics: Instantiate unit, stub dependencies, assert outputs/state. Keep tests independent and parallelizable.
unit testing.tradeoffs: Over-mocking tests implementation not behavior. Integration tests catch wiring issues unit tests miss.
unit testing.troubleshoot: Flakes: time/randomness/order dependence—freeze time and seed RNG. Fix by isolating side effects.
unit testing.integration: 1) Add tests around bugs. 2) Run in CI on every PR. 3) Keep unit suite < few minutes. 4) Pair with integration tests.

mock.summary: A mock/stub/fake replaces a dependency so tests control inputs and assert interactions without real I/O.
mock.problem: It keeps unit tests fast and focused when collaborators are slow or nondeterministic.
mock.mechanics: Inject a test double implementing the interface; configure return values; optionally assert called with args.
mock.tradeoffs: Too many mocks make tests brittle. Prefer fakes (in-memory DB) for richer behavior.
mock.troubleshoot: Tests pass but prod fails: doubles drifted from real contracts—add contract tests.
mock.example:
from unittest.mock import Mock
payments = Mock(); payments.charge.return_value = 'ok'
assert charge_order(payments, 10) == 'ok'
payments.charge.assert_called_once()
mock.integration: 1) Mock at boundaries only. 2) Prefer fakes for storage. 3) Add a contract test against real sandbox periodically.

continuous integration.summary: Continuous integration frequently merges work and runs automated builds/tests to detect integration failures early.
continuous integration.problem: It prevents long-lived branch hell and keeps main releasable.
continuous integration.mechanics: Each commit/PR triggers build+test(+lint). Failures block merge. Main stays green; fix forward or revert quickly.
continuous integration.tradeoffs: Slow pipelines reduce compliance. Over-heavy CI wastes compute—parallelize and cache.
continuous integration.troubleshoot: Flaky tests erode trust—quarantine with owners. Cache poisoning: key caches by lockfiles.
continuous integration.example:
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test
continuous integration.integration: 1) Require CI status on main. 2) Keep suite fast. 3) Ban flaky ignores without tickets. 4) Publish build artifacts.

relational model.summary: The relational model stores data as relations (tables) of tuples (rows) with typed attributes, queried declaratively with SQL.
relational model.problem: It provides a clear algebra for joins/filters and underpins ACID databases.
relational model.mechanics: Define schemas with keys/FKs; query with relational operators (select/project/join). Engine picks plans.
relational model.tradeoffs: Document DBs fit flexible hierarchies; warehouses may denormalize for analytics. Relational shines for integrity-heavy OLTP.
relational model.troubleshoot: Unexpected join fanout: check keys/cardinality. Use EXPLAIN.
relational model.example: SELECT u.name, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id;
relational model.integration: 1) Model entities/keys first. 2) Add FKs where integrity matters. 3) Index join/filter columns. 4) Review with EXPLAIN.

normalization.summary: Normalization organizes relational schemas to reduce redundancy and update anomalies (1NF/2NF/3NF/BCNF).
normalization.problem: It keeps each fact stored once so updates stay consistent.
normalization.mechanics: Identify keys and functional dependencies; decompose tables so non-keys depend only on keys. Denormalize later for read performance with clear sync rules.
normalization.tradeoffs: Over-normalization can force heavy joins; warehouses often denormalize. OLTP usually prefers higher normal forms.
normalization.troubleshoot: Update anomalies (same fact many places) signal under-normalization. Painful joins may justify materialized views.
normalization.example:
-- bad: orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_city)
-- better: customers(id,name,city); orders(id, customer_id)
